mcqs.question: A fixed window counter limits clients to 100 requests/minute. What is the real-world flaw this design has?
options: A client can send 100 requests at the end of one window and 100 more at the start of the next, hitting ~200 in a short span
It requires far more memory per client than any sliding window design
It cannot be implemented without a distributed lock across servers
It rejects all requests once any single client is throttled
mcqs.explanation: The counter resets to zero at each window boundary with no memory of the prior window, so two full quotas can land back-to-back across the edge. Memory usage is actually O(1), no distributed lock is inherently required, and throttling one client doesn't affect others.

mcqs.question: In a token bucket limiter, what do the `capacity` and `rate` parameters each control?
options: Capacity controls how many clients can be tracked; rate controls how often the tracking table is cleared
Capacity controls the maximum burst size a client can spend at once; rate controls the sustained long-run throughput
Capacity controls the sustained throughput; rate controls the maximum burst size
Both parameters control the same thing and only one needs to be set
mcqs.explanation: Capacity is the bucket's max size, so it bounds how big a single burst can be; rate is how fast it refills, which bounds the average rate over time. They're independent knobs, not the same thing, and swapping their described roles is the classic mix-up.

mcqs.question: You need to protect a downstream worker pool that truly cannot handle any burst, only a steady stream of work. Which algorithm fits best?
options: Fixed window counter, since it's the simplest to reason about
Sliding window log, since it gives an exact recent count
Leaky bucket, since it smooths output to a strictly constant rate regardless of input bursts
Token bucket, since it explicitly allows bursts up to capacity
mcqs.explanation: Leaky bucket queues requests and drains them at a fixed rate, so downstream never sees a burst — it only sees requests waiting longer. Token bucket is the wrong choice specifically because it lets bursts through; the two window counters don't control output rate at all.

mcqs.question: Your published SLA promises a hard cap with no more than a small, bounded overage ever, even across window edges. Which limiter design should you avoid?
options: Token bucket with a small capacity
Fixed window counter, because of its boundary double-spend
mcqs.explanation: Fixed window counter is the one design that can let a client spend a full quota twice within a short span across the reset boundary, breaking a hard-cap SLA. The other three all bound recent history rather than resetting sharply to zero.
